def: Temporal's name for a step that has side effects. Activities are separate functions that a workflow schedules; their results are recorded in the event history.
An error after a request was sent, where you can't tell whether the other side acted. A timeout is the classic example.
The guarantee durable execution gives each step's side effect: it runs at least once, and may run again if the process dies mid-step before the result is recorded.
Restate's way to pause until something outside the system (a person, a webhook) reports back with a result.
Waiting longer after each failed attempt before retrying (for example 0.5s, 1s, 2s, 4s), so retries don't overwhelm a struggling system.
A step that undoes an earlier step, such as a refund or releasing inventory. Used in sagas when a later step fails permanently.
A registered version of your service code at a specific URL or function version. In-flight invocations stay on the deployment they started on.
Given the same journal, workflow code asks for the same steps in the same order every time. Replay depends on it.
Survives a crash, because it's stored somewhere other than the program's memory.
A wait that survives crashes. The wake-up time is recorded, and in real platforms the server holds the timer so no process needs to stay running.
Temporal's name for the journal: the durable record of everything that happened in a workflow execution.
A stable, unique id attached to a request so the receiver can recognize a repeat and return the original result instead of acting twice.
An operation you can perform twice with the same effect as performing it once.
Restate's unit of work: one call to a handler, identified by an id starting with inv_, with its own journal.
The durable record of each completed step and its result, written before moving on. Restate's word; Temporal calls it the event history.
What an engine reports when replayed code asks for a different step than the journal recorded at that position, usually after a code change or a decision made outside a step.
Some steps of a process happened and others didn't, leaving the system in a state nobody designed for.
Restate's state for an invocation that has used up its retry attempts. It stops retrying and waits for a person to fix the cause and resume it.
Restate pushes work to your services by calling them; Temporal workers pull work by polling task queues. This shapes how each behaves when your code is down.
Re-running workflow code from the top after a crash, returning recorded results for finished steps instead of re-executing them.
A multi-step process that, when a step fails permanently, runs compensations to undo the steps that already succeeded.
A change outside the program, like a charge, a reservation or an email. Stopping the program doesn't undo it.
A message sent to a running Temporal workflow from outside, which the workflow can wait for and react to.
A sleeping or waiting workflow consumes no running process; the server wakes it when the timer fires or the event arrives.
In Temporal, a named queue that workers poll for work. If no worker polls it, work waits there silently.
An error the developer marks as permanent, so the engine stops retrying. Restate: TerminalError. Temporal: a non-retryable ApplicationFailure.
A failure that may go away if you try again later, like a 503 or a network blip.
Restate's durable entity: state stored per key (a cart, an account), with requests to the same key handled one at a time.
In Temporal, a process you run that polls a task queue and executes workflow and activity code.
A multi-step process run by a durable execution engine, identified by an id. In Restate, also a specific service type that runs exactly once per id.
